# LITs with `tags` `endosymbiosis`

*Topics — What a work is about. Nucleation holds whatever reading the owner files here, whether or not an Anthology of the SOTA topic could also hold it; instruction for ML practice belongs to the anthology (ADR-048). The words are seeded from the clusters the reading-time triage of 2026-09-25 found, and grow by decision.*

**Endosymbiosis and reductive evolution** — how one organism comes to live inside another and depend on it, and how that ends — reductive genome evolution by drift, deletional bias or adaptive loss (including the Black Queen dependencies of free-living microbes), complementary loss across partners, nested symbioses and symbiont splitting and replacement, endosymbiotic gene transfer, protein import and host control of transmission, organellogenesis and organelle loss, and eukaryogenesis. The ecology of a partnership is ecology (ADR-055).

| [LIT-1558](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1558.md) v3 | Dominant contribution of Asgard archaea to eukaryogenesis | Tobiasson, Luo, Wolf & Koonin (2026). Hypothesis tests on constrained trees for widespread eukaryotic genes traced to the last eukaryotic common ancestor give Asgard archaea about half of all likelihood weight in the best-resolved families and the lead in nearly every functional system. The alphaproteobacterial contribution is small and centred on the mitochondrion (oxidative phosphorylation, Fe–S cluster assembly, mitochondrial translation). About a third of families point to other bacteria, scattered across functions, which the authors read as piecemeal gene transfer and not further symbioses. A test of stem lengths finds they do not track acquisition time. The authors infer a complex Asgard ancestor that took up the mitochondrion late. | Active — read in full 2026-10-27 ([NOTE-1242](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1242.md)) from the PubMed Central copy of the version of record (PMC12872458, open access); worth reading as the largest survey so far of where the last eukaryotic common ancestor's genes came from, finding Asgard archaea the largest single source in nearly every functional system, the alphaproteobacterial share small and mitochondrial, and other bacteria diffuse ([THEORY-1104](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1104.md)), and for its test of the stem-length method, which it finds does not behave as a clock ([THEORY-1101](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1101.md)). Read it knowing that "dominant" means about half of likelihood weight among well-resolved families, not a count of genes; that the paper is itself mitochondrion-late; that its denial of further symbioses is read off the diffuseness of the bacterial signal, not shown; and that it rests on sparse, biased genome sampling, as the authors stress. |

| [LIT-1566](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1566.md) v3 | Dated gene duplications elucidate the evolutionary assembly of eukaryotes | Kay et al. (2026). A relaxed molecular clock dates 135 gene duplications on the two eukaryotic stem lineages, inside a species tree that puts the archaeal branch point at 3.05–2.79 billion years ago, the alphaproteobacterial one at 2.37–2.13 and LECA at 1.80–1.67. | [LIT-1568](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1568.md) v3 | The Black Queen Hypothesis: Evolution of Dependencies through Adaptive Gene Loss | Morris, Lenski & Zinser (2012). In free-living bacteria such as Prochlorococcus and Pelagibacter, loss of a costly, leaky function whose products are public goods is favoured at the individual level, and proceeds until production just suffices for the community, leaving the losers dependent on co-occurring helpers. Selection, not drift, makes the dependency. The one worked case is Prochlorococcus's loss of catalase-peroxidase (katG). | Active — read in full 2026-10-27 ([NOTE-1212](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1212.md)) from the PubMed Central copy of the version of record (PMC3315703, CC BY-NC-SA); worth reading as the selection route to microbial dependency, in which losing a costly, leaky function is favoured until helpers just supply the community ([THEORY-1048](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1048.md)). Read it knowing that it is an opinion piece with one worked case (katG in Prochlorococcus) whose benefit is computed, not measured; that it is stated for free-living microbes and credits drift for endosymbiont reduction; that its equations assume linear responses; and that its other examples and the "shooting the moon" acceleration are suggestions. |

| [LIT-1570](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1570.md) v3 | The Evolution of Dependence and Cohesion in Incipient Endosymbioses | Athreya, Czuppon & Gokhale (2025). An adaptive-dynamics model characterizes endosymbiosis by two collective properties, mutual dependence (survival as a collective) and reproductive cohesion (synchronized reproduction). The faster-growing partner becomes fully obligate first, and the other's dependence then stays, rises or falls with births and deaths inside the collective. Dependence evolves at all only if the collective's carrying capacity is high enough. Early on, dependence outruns cohesion, but only under the authors' chosen trait mapping, which their own appendix shows decides the result. | Active — read in full 2026-10-27 ([NOTE-1211](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1211.md)) from the bioRxiv preprint, version 2 of 2025-05-31 (CC BY-NC 4.0), not the version of record, which was not reached; worth reading as the first model to separate mutual dependence from reproductive cohesion in an incipient endosymbiosis, with logistic growth for host, symbiont and collective, and for its results that the faster-evolving partner becomes obligate first and that the other's fate turns on births and deaths inside the collective ([THEORY-1051](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1051.md)). Read it knowing that its headline result, dependence evolving ahead of cohesion, is fixed by the authors' choice of how traits enter free growth and dissociation and reverses under the opposite choice in their own appendix ([THEORY-1050](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1050.md)); that nothing is tested against data, as the authors say; and that obligacy is a phenomenological trade-off, not gene loss. |

| [LIT-1590](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1590.md) v2 | Changes in Endosymbiont Complexity Drive Host-Level Compensatory Adaptations in Cicadas | Campbell et al. (2018). Where Hodgkinia has split into essential lineages of very uneven abundance, rare lineages risk loss at the transmission bottleneck from mother to egg, and a simulation shows the cells needed per egg rising steeply with complexity. Counts in eggs of four cicada species find Sulcia roughly constant and Hodgkinia up to about six times higher in Magicicada septendecim than in a single-lineage species, though only that species differs significantly. Every sampled egg carried every tracked lineage, and the transmission route looks unchanged. The authors read the raised titre as host compensation and a cost of fragmentation, and speculate that it could feed further splitting. | Active — read in full 2026-10-27 ([NOTE-1235](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1235.md)) from the PubMed Central copy of the version of record (PMC6234865, CC BY 4.0); worth reading as the record's one documented case of a host compensating for its symbiont's changes at transmission: cicadas whose Hodgkinia has split into many lineages send more Hodgkinia cells to each egg, not more Sulcia, and every sampled egg carried every tracked lineage ([THEORY-1106](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1106.md)). Read it knowing that the rise in titre is significant for one species, Magicicada septendecim, of four compared, with five or six eggs each and no phylogenetic control; that the six-lineage species does not differ significantly from single-lineage ones; that lineage presence was tracked by one or two marker genes; and that the order of cause, splitting before titre, is inferred. |
| [LIT-1591](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1591.md) v2 | Isolation of an archaeon at the prokaryote–eukaryote interface | Imachi et al. (2020). After 12 years from sampling to culture, an Asgard archaeon related to Lokiarchaeota, Candidatus Prometheoarchaeum syntrophicum MK-D1, was obtained in stable co-culture with a methanogen. From its genome and other Asgard genomes the authors infer that the Asgard ancestor was a partner-dependent amino-acid degrader, and they propose the entangle–engulf–endogenize model of eukaryogenesis as a hypothesis. | Active — read in full 2026-10-27 ([NOTE-1238](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1238.md)) from the PubMed Central copy of the version of record (PMC7015854, CC BY 4.0); worth reading as the first physiology of an Asgard archaeon, a small, internally simple coccus with branching protrusions that grows only in syntrophy, handing hydrogen and formate to partners that can be exchanged, and for the authors' inference that the Asgard ancestor was likewise partner-dependent ([THEORY-1108](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1108.md)). Read it knowing that the organism was grown only in co-culture, never alone; that it is the closest relative of eukaryotes among cultured organisms only; that the ancestral lifestyle is inferred from gene presence in metagenome-assembled genomes; that the entangle–engulf–endogenize model is, in the authors' words, hypothetical and not definitive; and that the model is not the hydrogen hypothesis, since here the host makes the hydrogen. |
| [LIT-1595](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1595.md) v2 | Late acquisition of mitochondria by a host with chimaeric prokaryotic ancestry | Pittis & Gabaldón (2016). For 1,078 protein families inferred in the last eukaryotic common ancestor, the branch to the closest prokaryotic relatives, corrected for each family's rate, is shortest for families of alphaproteobacterial origin and mitochondrial location, longer for other bacterial families, which associate with endomembranes, and longest for archaeal families, which associate with the nucleus. The authors read this as late acquisition of the mitochondrion by a host whose genome already held genes of several bacterial origins, by partners or by transfer. The reading of length as time assumes proportional rates before and after LECA, and the alphaproteobacterial difference from other bacteria is P = 0.044. | Active — read in full 2026-10-27 ([NOTE-1240](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1240.md)) from the PubMed Central author manuscript (PMC4780264), not the version of record; worth reading as the first proteome-wide test of mitochondrion-early against mitochondrion-late, and for its finding that LECA families sort by origin and cell location (alphaproteobacterial with the mitochondrion, other bacterial with endomembranes, archaeal with the nucleus), with alphaproteobacterial families nearest their prokaryotic relatives ([THEORY-1102](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1102.md)). Read it knowing that stem length is read as time only under the assumption that rates before and after LECA are proportional; that the alphaproteobacterial difference from other bacteria, on which the chimaeric host turns, is P = 0.044; that stem length also shortens when a closer relative is sampled, as its own Lokiarchaeota control shows; and that it cannot say whether the chimaera came from partners or from gene transfer. |
| [LIT-1596](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1596.md) v2 | Genome sequence of the endocellular bacterial symbiont of aphids Buchnera sp. APS | Shigenobu et al. (2000). The first complete genome of an obligate insect endosymbiont: Buchnera sp. APS, maternally transmitted in aphid bacteriocytes, has a 640,681-bp chromosome with 583 ORFs and two small plasmids, a subset of E. coli's gene set reached by loss. It keeps the genes for the amino acids essential to the host and lacks almost all of those for non-essential ones, and uses host-made glutamate and aspartate as precursors, so the two partners' pathways interlock. It also lacks phospholipid and lipopolysaccharide synthesis, nearly all transcriptional regulators, and recA and uvrABC. The authors infer that it can live only in the bacteriocyte, with membrane lipids perhaps from the host, and compare it to an organelle. All of this is read from gene content. | Active — read in full 2026-10-27 ([NOTE-1236](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1236.md)) from the publisher's free PDF of the version of record; worth reading as the first complete genome of an obligate insect endosymbiont, and for its gene-by-gene account of a symbiont that keeps the amino-acid pathways its host lacks, draws precursors from the host, and has lost phospholipid synthesis and nearly all its own regulators ([THEORY-1103](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1103.md)). Read it knowing that every functional statement is inferred from gene content in one strain, that the host's dependence is cited from earlier work and maternal transmission stated, neither shown here, and that it names no mechanism of genome reduction: drift and Muller's ratchet are not in it. |
